bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, beyond the quarter-mile ring, on slab and talus. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
bivy.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
bivy.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

bivy.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.
bivy.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
bivy.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
bivy.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

bivy.name: Middle Peak crest bivouac, Mount Index traverse
bivy.notes: The traverse of Mount Index's three peaks is the one objective in this zone that is genuinely an overnight rather than a long day, and this is where parties sleep. The line links South, Middle and North Peaks along a crest of loose ridges and gullies with rappels between them, and the recorded practice is a flat spot right on the crest between the two Middle Peak summits with snow nearby, which solves the water problem in early season. Parties who have done it in a push describe going light and treating the bivouac as an emergency plan that they were glad to have and glad not to need — take minimal gear rather than a full camp, because everything you carry has to come over some genuinely poor rock. Approach is the Lake Serene trail as for everything else on the mountain. The rock on Index is famously rotten and the descent options off the ridge are limited, so committing to a bivouac here means committing to finishing the traverse; do not plan it as a place to sit out bad weather.
bivy.water: Snow on the crest into early summer, and nothing at all once it goes. On a dry traverse you carry water for the whole ridge or you drop off it.
bivy.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the ridge. The trailhead day-use rules below still apply to the car. Fires are out of the question up here regardless of the current ban.
bivy.capacity: One small party. A flat patch on the ridge crest between the two Middle Peak summits — a stance, not a site.

approach: From the White Chuck River Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of White Chuck River Road/FR 23), follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) upstream through old-growth forest. The trail fords/bridges several tributaries — Pumice Creek, Glacier Creek, and Kennedy Creek — which serve as reliable water sources but can run high with snowmelt in early summer. At about 5.5 miles reach the former Kennedy Hot Springs/Kennedy Guard Station area (~3,300 ft) — still a popular campsite, but the historic hot-springs pool, lodge, and guard station were destroyed and buried by the October 2003 flood/debris flow and were never rebuilt; there is no usable hot pool here. Continue roughly 1.5 miles farther to Sitkum Creek and the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (~3,850 ft). Turn north (left) on the PCT for about a half mile to a forested campsite near 4,100 ft — a common lower camp. From there, leave the maintained trail and follow a steep, unmaintained climbers' path (locally described as 'more like a fisherman's route than a trail') straight up the forested ridge to Boulder Basin (5,500–6,000 ft), where the trees break and the standard high camp sits on heather/rock benches with running water nearby. From camp, ascend snowfields southeast/uphill onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. Note: the White Chuck River Road and Trail sustained major washout damage in the October 2003 floods and has had repeated closures/repairs since — confirm current road-end and trail status with the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest before relying on this approach, as in bad years the effective trailhead moves miles downstream.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required for parking. No climbing permits or camping fees required. Trail status: The White Chuck River Trail was severely damaged by a 2003 flood; contact Darrington Ranger Station for current conditions.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) in Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft.
access.seasonal: Mountain Loop Highway has a seasonal gate closure (Deer Creek–Bedal, ~14 mi), typically Nov–mid/late May. Suiattle River Road (FSR 26), the primary Glacier Peak access, has had storm-damage closures — check current conditions before a trip.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

approach: From the White Chuck River Trailhead (end of FR 23, ~2,300 ft, reached from Darrington), follow White Chuck River Trail #643 up-valley through old-growth and second-growth forest along the White Chuck River. There are several tributary creek crossings (some bridged, some not) in the first few miles — treat them with caution in early season or after rain. At roughly 5.5-6 miles you reach the site of the old Kennedy Hot Springs / Kennedy Guard Station (~3,300 ft); the springs themselves were largely buried by debris in the 2003 flood and there are no facilities, but it remains a natural rest/camp point. Continue about 1.5 miles farther, fording Sitkum Creek, to the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (~3,850 ft) — this crossing can run high with snowmelt in June/July. At the PCT junction, look for a cairn marking the start of the unmaintained but well-trodden 'Sitkum Trail' climbers' path, which switchbacks steeply east up a forested-to-heather ridge, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in a little over a mile, to the campsites of Boulder Basin (~5,700 ft) — the standard base camp, with reliable water from snowmelt tarns and streams through midsummer. Total distance to Boulder Basin is roughly 9-11 miles with 4,000-4,500 ft of gain. From Boulder Basin the route goes cross-country and onto glacier: head southeast onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier, staying in the corridor left (north) of the rock rib/icefall that splits the lower glacier, then trend northeast up-glacier to a broad saddle at approximately 9,500 ft immediately east of Sitkum Spire. The upper Sitkum Glacier carries real crevasse hazard in both its lower and upper sections — rope up for glacier travel, carry standard crevasse-rescue gear, and expect more open crevasses by late summer. From the saddle, a short, loose pumice-and-rock ridge scramble (class 2-3 with a class 3-4 step near the top) leads to the summit block of Sitkum Spire itself. Route-finding on the broad, featureless summit plateau and glacier can be tricky in flat light or whiteout — a GPS track or careful compass bearing is worthwhile. Note separately that FR 23 access to the White Chuck River Trailhead has a history of washouts/closures (2003 flood, and more recent 2025 flood damage) and should be checked for current status before relying on this approach.

access.fees: No fee or permit charge to climb or camp — a free self-issue wilderness permit is completed at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass is required to park at the trailhead.
access.rules: Standard Glacier Peak Wilderness rules: campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft elevation (effectively all of this route), camp at least 200 ft from water and trails where possible, and pack out all trash.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register; no quota or reservation required.
access.closures: As of the 2026 season, FS Road 23 (White Chuck River Road) is closed by Forest Order #06-05-25-02 from milepost 3.7 to its end at the FS Road 27 (Rat Trap Pass) junction, due to flood damage — this adds roughly 7 miles (14 round trip) of road-walking to the approach. Note: this closure order took effect March 19, 2025 (originally through Dec 31, 2025, and still active per spring 2026 NF alerts), so it predates and is unrelated to the separate, much larger December 2025 Pacific Northwest atmospheric-river floods — the road damage behind this order is from an earlier storm. Separately, White Chuck River Trail #643 and Kennedy Hot Springs have never been fully rebuilt since the October 2003 flood destroyed the springs and buried sections of trail, so the route between the old trailhead and Sitkum Creek remains rough, brushy, and involves unbridged crossings. Check current Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alerts before heading out, as access has changed repeatedly over the past two decades.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (within the Glacier Peak Wilderness).
